title: The Gifts of Imperfection
source_note: Book not read; DB title 'Özgür Olmak 2' mapped to The Gifts of Imperfection from content (perfectionism, shame/guilt, joy). Facts from summaries, search snippets and memory of the book; confidence marked.

facts.claim: Subtitle: Let Go of Who You Think You're Supposed to Be and Embrace Who You Are. Ten guideposts, each pairing something to cultivate with something to let go of.
Perfectionism is a twenty-ton shield we lug around thinking it protects us, when it prevents us from taking flight.
Perfectionism: if I look perfect, do everything perfectly, act perfectly, I can minimise or avoid shame, judgment and blame; a defensive strategy, not drive for excellence.
Perfectionism is other-focused ('What will people think?'); healthy striving is self-focused ('How can I improve?').
Perfectionism sits under self-compassion ('letting go of perfectionism') among the guideposts.
When shame, judgment or blame come anyway, perfectionists often blame not being perfect enough, which feeds the cycle.
Shame: intensely painful feeling of believing we are flawed and unworthy of love and belonging; 'I am bad'. Guilt: 'I did something bad'.
Guilt holds a behaviour against our values and can motivate positive change; shame is associated with addiction, aggression, depression, violence.
Apology contrast: 'I'm sorry. I made a mistake.' vs 'I'm sorry. I am a mistake.'
facts.source: fs.blog page on Brown; exact book location unconfirmed

facts.claim: Shame grows in secrecy and silence and 'hates having words wrapped around it'; the book offers four shame-resilience steps.
Guidepost 4: Cultivating Gratitude and Joy: Letting Go of Scarcity and Fear of the Dark.
In her research Brown never met someone able to feel joy without regularly practicing gratitude.
facts.source: Oprah interview via search summary; book wording unconfirmed

facts.claim: Foreboding joy: when joy arrives, many people feel fear of loss and imagine catastrophe; a parent looking at a child; joyful people respond by practicing gratitude.
facts.source: ursummary; search results (sources disagree on which book first uses the term)

facts.claim: We cannot numb painful emotions selectively; numbing the dark also numbs joy and gratitude.
Brown analysed thousands of interviews and split people into those living with worthiness and those who struggled.
